Purpose: to compare the hardness of tap water and bottled water.
Materials: two clear jars, a measuring cup, liquid soap, a timer.
Procedure: (1) Label the jars A (tap) and B (bottled). (2) Pour exactly 200 mL of water into each jar. (3) Add three drops of soap to each jar. (4) Close the lids and shake each jar for 15 seconds. (5) Wait one minute, then measure the height of the bubbles. Hard water makes fewer bubbles.

options: to make the test fair so only the type of water changes
because 200 mL is the largest amount that the jars can hold
so the jars look the same on the shelf for the visitors
to save soap and water for the next class to use
questions.why: Using the same amount keeps the test fair; only the kind of water is different.

She forgot Arabic after living abroad for many years, so she only speaks English.
Bayt represents an emotional homeland, while house is just a place she lives.
questions.why: The last sentence explains the emotional difference.

questions.passage: My grandmother has two words for home. In Arabic she says bayt, and her voice softens as if remembering a courtyard and a fig tree. In English she says house, quickly, the way you name a bus stop. I used to think she simply preferred the old language. Now I understand she has two homes, and only one of them is a building.
questions.stem: How does the author use language to show cultural experience?
options: By describing a bus stop in detail, the author shows the street where the family waits for a ride every morning.
By translating every word she says into English, the author makes the whole story easy for all readers to follow.
By listing Arabic words on a page, the author gives readers a long vocabulary list without any story at all.
By contrasting how the grandmother says each word, the author shows deeper meaning in her first language.
questions.why: Tone of voice reveals cultural attachment.

questions.passage: My grandmother has two words for home. In Arabic she says bayt, and her voice softens as if remembering a courtyard and a fig tree. In English she says house, quickly, the way you name a bus stop. I used to think she simply preferred the old language. Now I understand she has two homes, and only one of them is a building.
questions.stem: How does the narrator's point of view change?
options: From an English speaker to an Arabic speaker as she grows older in the big city.
It does not change at all from the beginning to the end of the story.
From loving the grandmother to hating her because she speaks Arabic at home.
From thinking it is a language preference to understanding it as a sense of belonging.
questions.why: Used to think... Now I understand shows the change.

sets.skill: Sound Devices: Alliteration, Onomatopoeia and Repetition

questions.stem: Which sentence uses alliteration (the same first sound repeated)?
options: The dog ran home to its bed.
I like to read at night.
Silly snakes slide slowly.
It is cold outside today.
questions.why: Silly, snakes, slide and slowly all begin with s.

questions.stem: Which word is an example of onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like what it means)?
options: table
happy
green
buzz
questions.why: Buzz sounds like a bee.

questions.stem: In the line "Run, run, as fast as you can," why is run repeated?
options: to show the character is sleepy and slow
to name a place on the map of town
to show speed and make the line catchy
because the writer made a mistake in it
questions.why: Repetition adds rhythm and shows action.

questions.stem: "The thunder crashed and the rain went splish, splash, splat." Which words are onomatopoeia?
options: crashed, splish, splash, splat
thunder, rain
went
the, and
questions.why: These words imitate sounds.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the alliteration in "The wild wind whistled through the willows"?
options: It tells the time of day in the story, at dawn.
It imitates the sound of blowing wind.
It shows the wind stopped before the night began.
It explains what willows are to young readers.
questions.why: The repeated w sound sounds like wind.

questions.stem: In a poem, the line "I will not quit" appears at the end of each stanza. What is the effect?
options: It emphasizes the speaker's determination.
It shows the poem is ending early and is almost over.
It confuses the reader about the main idea.
It describes the setting of the poem.
questions.why: Repetition stresses an important idea.

questions.stem: "Crackle and creak, the cold ice cracked beneath their careful feet." What effect do the sound devices create?
options: They make the scene calm and quiet, like a sleepy night.
They describe the characters' clothing and their warm coats.
They show it is summer and the sun is very hot.
They make the reader hear the ice breaking and feel the danger.
questions.why: Hard c sounds and onomatopoeia mimic cracking ice.

questions.stem: A speech repeats "We will remember" at the start of four sentences. What is the MOST likely purpose?
options: to show uncertainty
to build emotional force and unity
to fill time
to introduce a new topic each time
questions.why: Repetition at the start of sentences (anaphora) builds emotion.

questions.stem: Which line uses both alliteration and onomatopoeia?
options: Rain fell on the roof of the house.
The busy bees buzzed beside the blooms.
We walked home at noon with our friends.
The sun set slowly behind the hills.
questions.why: Repeated b sounds plus the sound word buzzed.

questions.stem: Hot is to cold as up is to ____.
options: sky
high
down
warm
questions.why: Hot and cold are opposites; the opposite of up is down.

questions.stem: Bird is to nest as bee is to ____.
options: flower
hive
honey
wing
questions.why: A bird lives in a nest; a bee lives in a hive.

questions.stem: Puppy is to dog as kitten is to ____.
options: mouse
cat
toy
milk
questions.why: A puppy is a young dog; a kitten is a young cat.

questions.stem: Author is to book as composer is to ____.
options: paint
music
story
piano
questions.why: An author creates a book; a composer creates music.

questions.stem: Pen is to write as scissors are to ____.
options: sharp
paper
glue
cut
questions.why: The analogy shows what each tool is used for.

questions.stem: Petal is to flower as page is to ____.
options: word
book
read
paper
questions.why: A petal is part of a flower; a page is part of a book.

questions.stem: Drought is to rain as famine is to ____.
options: desert
hunger
farm
food
questions.why: A drought is a lack of rain; a famine is a lack of food.

questions.stem: Timid is to bold as frugal is to ____.
options: poor
wasteful
careful
quiet
questions.why: Both pairs are opposites; frugal means careful with money.

questions.stem: A writer says: "Memory is a library where some books have been checked out forever." What does this analogy suggest?
options: Some memories are lost and cannot be recovered.
Libraries store memories from people's brains.
Books are hard to read in a library.
Memories are always clear and never fade.
questions.why: Books checked out forever stand for forgotten memories.

questions.passage: Every spring, Dad and Sara flew a red kite together. After Dad moved away for work, Sara kept the kite by her bed. When he came home, she ran to him with the kite in her hands.
questions.stem: What does the red kite most likely stand for?
options: a toy store in the town square
Sara's special bond with her dad
windy weather over the hills and fields
spring flowers in the garden of her home
questions.why: The kite represents their time together.

questions.passage: Every spring, Dad and Sara flew a red kite together. After Dad moved away for work, Sara kept the kite by her bed. When he came home, she ran to him with the kite in her hands.
questions.stem: Why does Sara keep the kite by her bed?
options: It is broken and cannot fly.
She does not like it any more.
It reminds her of her dad.
It is new and was a gift.
questions.why: It helps her feel close to him.

questions.passage: Every spring, Dad and Sara flew a red kite together. After Dad moved away for work, Sara kept the kite by her bed. When he came home, she ran to him with the kite in her hands.
questions.stem: A symbol is—
options: an object that stands for an idea
a type of poem with short lines
a long word that is hard to say
the title of a story in a book
questions.why: Symbols represent ideas.

questions.passage: Throughout the novel, Amira's bedroom door stays locked. After she makes her first real friend at school, she leaves it open for the first time.
questions.stem: What does the locked door most likely symbolize?
options: Amira closing herself off from others
her messy room with the clothes on the floor
a broken lock on the door of the house
a family rule about being home before dark
questions.why: The locked door shows she keeps people out.

questions.passage: Throughout the novel, Amira's bedroom door stays locked. After she makes her first real friend at school, she leaves it open for the first time.
questions.stem: What does leaving the door open symbolize?
options: her new willingness to let people in
her room is clean and tidy now
she forgot to lock it before she left
she is moving to a new house soon
questions.why: Opening the door matches opening up to friendship.

questions.passage: Throughout the novel, Amira's bedroom door stays locked. After she makes her first real friend at school, she leaves it open for the first time.
questions.stem: Why do authors use symbols like the door?
options: to describe houses and doors in a lot of detail
to show changes in characters without stating them directly
to confuse readers and hide the real story from them
to fill space on the page so that the book looks much longer
questions.why: Symbols show meaning indirectly.

questions.passage: In the story, the town's broken clock tower has shown 3:10 for forty years, the moment the factory closed. The townspeople have stopped noticing it. At the end, a group of teenagers repairs the clock, and its bells ring across the square for the first time in decades.
questions.stem: What does the stopped clock most likely symbolize?
options: a town stuck in the past after the factory closed
a holiday that the whole town enjoys each year
bad engineering by the people who made it
the exact time of day in the story's town
questions.why: Time frozen at the closing shows the town never moved on.

questions.passage: In the story, the town's broken clock tower has shown 3:10 for forty years, the moment the factory closed. The townspeople have stopped noticing it. At the end, a group of teenagers repairs the clock, and its bells ring across the square for the first time in decades.
questions.stem: What does the teenagers' repair of the clock suggest?
options: The factory reopened at 3:10 on a Monday morning.
The teenagers want to leave the town and never return.
Clocks are easy to fix with a few simple tools.
A new generation is helping the town move forward.
questions.why: Restarting time suggests renewal.

questions.passage: In the story, the town's broken clock tower has shown 3:10 for forty years, the moment the factory closed. The townspeople have stopped noticing it. At the end, a group of teenagers repairs the clock, and its bells ring across the square for the first time in decades.
questions.stem: Why is it significant that the townspeople stopped noticing the clock?
options: It shows they were busy at work all day.
It suggests they had accepted being stuck.
It means the clock was hidden by a tall tree.
It shows the clock was quiet and never rang.
questions.why: Not noticing shows acceptance of stagnation.

questions.stem: What does the word careless mean?
options: care again
one who cares
full of care
without care
questions.why: The suffix -less means without.

questions.stem: A teacher is a person who ____.
options: teaches
does not teach
is taught
teaches again
questions.why: The suffix -er can mean a person who does something.

questions.stem: What does reread mean?
options: read slowly
read again
not read
read before
questions.why: The prefix re- means again.

questions.stem: Which word means full of hope?
options: hopeful
rehope
hoper
hopeless
questions.why: -ful means full of.

questions.stem: An artist is someone who—
options: makes art
looks at art
has no art
sells paint
questions.why: -ist means a person who does something.

questions.stem: Which word means one who visits?
options: revisit
visitless
visitor
visitful
questions.why: -or means a person who does an action.

questions.stem: The scientist reexamined the fossil and found it belonged to a fearless predator. Which word means examined again?
options: predator
reexamined
scientist
fearless
questions.why: re- + examined = examined again.

questions.stem: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The ____ tested the new medicine in her lab."
options: chemful
chemless
chemist
rechem
questions.why: -ist names a person who works in a field.

questions.stem: Which pair shows opposite meanings created by suffixes?
options: useful / useless
teacher / actor
painter / pianist
redo / reread
questions.why: -ful (full of) and -less (without) are opposites.

questions.stem: Which word is a compound word?
options: tiger
sunflower
running
happy
questions.why: Sun + flower makes sunflower.

questions.stem: What two words make the word rainbow?
options: rainb + ow
rai + nbow
rain + bow
ra + inbow
questions.why: Rainbow combines rain and bow.

questions.stem: What is a toothbrush?
options: a tooth that brushes
a paint brush
a kind of hair
a brush for your teeth
questions.why: The two smaller words explain the meaning.

questions.stem: Use the two smaller words to figure out the meaning of bookworm.
options: a bookshelf for old books
a torn book with loose pages
a person who loves to read
a worm that lives in a garden
questions.why: Like a worm in books, a bookworm reads all the time.

questions.stem: Which compound word means the place where the sun comes up and the start of the day?
options: sunrise
sunburn
sunlight
sunset
questions.why: Sun + rise.

questions.stem: Which word is NOT a compound word?
options: football
remember
notebook
airport
questions.why: Remember is not made of two smaller words.

questions.stem: In "The new law was a breakthrough for workers," what does breakthrough mean?
options: a mistake
an important advance
a broken wall
a fast run
questions.why: Breaking through a barrier suggests an important advance.

questions.stem: Which compound word best completes: "After the storm, the ____ of the bridge was clear—it needed to be rebuilt."
options: downside
upside
inside
outside
questions.why: Downside means disadvantage.

questions.stem: What does the compound word heartfelt mean in "She gave a heartfelt thank-you"?
options: a heart that is hurt
sincere and deeply felt
felt fabric
fast
questions.why: Felt in the heart means sincere.

questions.stem: Which word belongs in the group: apple, banana, grape, ____?
options: dog
chair
carrot
orange
questions.why: All are fruits.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a tool?
options: river
pizza
hammer
cloud
questions.why: A hammer is a tool.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT belong: red, blue, green, happy?
options: happy
blue
green
red
questions.why: Happy is a feeling, not a color.

questions.stem: Which word names a category that includes eagle, owl and parrot?
options: insects
pets
animals that swim
birds
questions.why: They are all birds.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a mammal?
options: whale
shark
frog
lizard
questions.why: Whales are mammals.

questions.stem: Which group is sorted correctly under the category instruments?
options: drum, desk, harp
violin, spoon, flute
flute, apple, trumpet
violin, drum, flute
questions.why: All three are instruments.

questions.stem: Which word is the most general category for the others: democracy, monarchy, dictatorship, government?
options: government
monarchy
dictatorship
democracy
questions.why: The others are types of government.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a renewable resource?
options: natural gas
oil
wind
coal
questions.why: Wind is renewable; the others are fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT belong with the others: persuade, convince, influence, ignore?
options: convince
persuade
ignore
influence
questions.why: The others mean to get someone to think or act a certain way.

questions.stem: Which word shows where the cat is? "The cat is under the table."
options: under
cat
is
table
questions.why: Under tells the position.

questions.stem: Which word shows a contrast? "I wanted to play outside, but it was raining."
options: but
outside
raining
wanted
questions.why: But shows the opposite idea.

questions.stem: Which word tells position? "The bird sat above the window."
options: above
window
bird
sat
questions.why: Above tells where.

questions.stem: Which word signals contrast in the sentence? "Although the test was hard, Sami finished early."
options: Although
test
early
hard
questions.why: Although introduces a contrasting idea.

questions.stem: Which phrase describes a spatial relationship? "The library is located between the bank and the park."
options: the bank
The library
between the bank and the park
is located
questions.why: Between shows position.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the contrast? "The desert is hot in the day; ____, it is cold at night."
options: also
because
so
however
questions.why: However shows contrast.

questions.stem: Which transition shows contrast most precisely? "Many experts praised the plan; ____, several engineers warned of hidden costs."
options: similarly
for example
nevertheless
therefore
questions.why: Nevertheless introduces a contrasting point.

questions.stem: In "The village lay adjacent to the river, opposite the old mill," what do adjacent and opposite describe?
options: the age of the mill by the river
the size of the wide river
the position of the village
the time of day in the story
questions.why: They tell where the village is.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a contrast word correctly?
options: Because despite rain the match.
Despite the rain, the match continued.
Despite the rain, so the match ended.
The match continued despite.
questions.why: Despite + noun shows contrast correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the sense of smell?
options: The car was red and very shiny.
The bell rang loudly at the school gate.
We walked home slowly after the long day.
The bread smelled warm and sweet.
questions.why: Smelled appeals to smell.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a loud sound?
options: quiet
soft
gentle
booming
questions.why: Booming means very loud.

questions.stem: Which sentence helps you picture the scene best?
options: The chick moved to the other side of the yard slowly.
The tiny yellow chick hopped across the green grass.
There was grass in the garden near the house and the road.
It was a chick, and it was small and nice to see.
questions.why: Descriptive words help readers picture it.

questions.stem: Which sense does this sentence appeal to? "The ice cream was so cold it made my teeth ache."
options: sight
touch and taste
smell
hearing
questions.why: Cold and teeth aching relate to touch and taste.

questions.stem: Which word is more precise than walked in "The tired runner walked to the finish"?
options: moved
went
did
staggered
questions.why: Staggered shows tired, unsteady walking.

questions.stem: What does the description "The wind howled like a wolf" help the reader understand?
options: the wind was gentle and quiet
the wind was loud and wild
a wolf was nearby in the forest
it was sunny and very hot
questions.why: It compares the wind's sound to a howling wolf.

questions.stem: Which phrase uses sensory language to create a tense mood?
options: she walked upstairs
the house had two floors
the stairs were wooden
the floorboards groaned under each slow step
questions.why: Groaning boards create sound and tension.

questions.stem: Which word best replaces said to show anger? "'Leave now,' he said."
options: giggled
asked
snapped
whispered
questions.why: Snapped shows a sharp, angry tone.

questions.stem: How does sensory detail strengthen this sentence? "The market was a riot of saffron, smoke and shouting."
options: It gives the market's history and the year that it was built.
It combines sight, smell and sound to make the busy market vivid.
It describes a quiet place with very few people in it.
It lists prices of the fruit and spices that were sold.
questions.why: Several senses create a vivid scene.

questions.stem: What does it mean when someone says "It's raining cats and dogs"?
options: Animals are falling from the sky.
It is sunny and hot, no clouds.
Pets are playing in the rain.
It is raining very hard.
questions.why: This idiom means heavy rain.

questions.stem: "Hold your horses!" means—
options: ride a horse
run fast
hold an animal
wait a moment
questions.why: It means slow down or wait.

questions.stem: If something is "a piece of cake," it is—
options: hard
sweet
easy
broken
questions.why: The idiom means very easy.

questions.stem: "Maya was on cloud nine after she won." What does on cloud nine mean?
options: very tired
very happy
confused
in the sky
questions.why: The phrase means extremely happy.

questions.stem: "Don't spill the beans about the party." What does spill the beans mean?
options: clean up
tell a secret
cook dinner
drop food
questions.why: It means reveal a secret.

questions.stem: "Learning chess was an uphill battle for Leo." What does an uphill battle mean?
options: a sports match
a game on a hill
a difficult struggle
an easy task
questions.why: It describes something hard to do.

questions.stem: "The new manager had to hit the ground running." What does this phrase mean?
options: start working quickly and energetically
arrive very late and very slowly
fall down flat on the hard ground
go jogging slowly in the big park now
questions.why: It means begin with full effort right away.

questions.stem: "Her proposal was met with a cold shoulder." What does cold shoulder mean?
options: a warm welcome from a friendly neighbor
a medical problem with the muscles of the arm
a chilly room that is very cold in winter
deliberate unfriendliness or rejection
questions.why: It means being ignored or rejected.

questions.stem: "The team's victory was bittersweet because their captain was injured." What does bittersweet mean?
options: confusing, hard to follow
both happy and sad
only sad about it
very tasty, sweet
questions.why: Bittersweet mixes joy and sadness.

questions.stem: In "I can see the bat flying at night," what does bat mean?
options: a baseball tool
a hat
to hit
an animal
questions.why: Flying at night tells us it is the animal.

questions.stem: In "Please turn on the light," what does light mean?
options: to start a small fire
a lamp or brightness
pale in color and soft
not heavy to carry
questions.why: Turn on shows it is a lamp.

questions.stem: In "The ring on her finger shines," what does ring mean?
options: the sound of a bell
a boxing area for fights
jewelry worn on a finger
a circle of people
questions.why: On her finger shows jewelry.

questions.stem: In "The scientist will present her findings," what does present mean?
options: show now, at once to all
here, in this place
show or explain to others
a gift for a friend
questions.why: Present findings means show them.

questions.stem: In "The judge will sentence him tomorrow," what does sentence mean?
options: a short story
a group of words
to write
give a punishment
questions.why: Judges sentence people to punishments.

questions.stem: In "The country's leader will address the nation," what does address mean?
options: speak to
a home location
a letter
a computer link
questions.why: Address the nation means speak to it.

questions.stem: In "The committee will table the proposal until next month," what does table mean?
options: a piece of furniture
a chart of data
to eat
postpone discussion
questions.why: To table can mean delay.

questions.stem: In "Her argument lacked substance," what does substance mean?
options: a weight
a chemical
a physical material
meaningful content
questions.why: It means real content or depth.

questions.stem: In "The novel's central conceit is that time runs backward," what does conceit mean?
options: an imaginative idea or device
too much pride in oneself and one's work
a lie told to a friend or a teacher
a trick question on a test in class
questions.why: In literature, a conceit is a central imaginative idea.

questions.stem: Where would you look to find the meaning of a word?
options: a calendar
a map
a dictionary
a menu
questions.why: Dictionaries give word meanings.

questions.stem: Which word would come first in a dictionary?
options: cherry
apple
date
banana
questions.why: Dictionaries are in alphabetical order.

questions.stem: Where would you find a word that means the same as happy?
options: a thesaurus
an atlas
a phone book
a recipe book
questions.why: A thesaurus lists synonyms.

questions.passage: glow (glō) verb 1. to give off a steady light without flames. 2. to look warm or bright with health or happiness. noun 3. a soft, steady light.
questions.stem: Which meaning of glow is used in "Her face glowed with pride"?
options: meaning 2
meaning 3
none
meaning 1
questions.why: Her face looking bright with happiness matches meaning 2.

questions.passage: glow (glō) verb 1. to give off a steady light without flames. 2. to look warm or bright with health or happiness. noun 3. a soft, steady light.
questions.stem: What part of speech is glow in meaning 3?
options: adjective
noun
verb
adverb
questions.why: Meaning 3 is labeled noun.

questions.passage: glow (glō) verb 1. to give off a steady light without flames. 2. to look warm or bright with health or happiness. noun 3. a soft, steady light.
questions.stem: What does (glō) show?
options: how to pronounce the word
the word's origin and its history
its plural form in a sentence
a synonym that is close in meaning
questions.why: Pronunciation is shown in parentheses.

questions.stem: A student is writing about ancient Rome and needs the precise meaning of the word aqueduct as historians use it. Which source is MOST useful?
options: a general children's thesaurus
a specialized history glossary
a calendar
a rhyming dictionary
questions.why: A specialized glossary gives field-specific meanings.

questions.stem: A writer has used the word important five times and wants variety. Which resource helps most?
options: an atlas
a thesaurus
an encyclopedia index
a phone directory
questions.why: A thesaurus suggests synonyms like significant or essential.

questions.stem: Which detail in a dictionary entry helps you find the word's history?
options: the guide words
the pronunciation
the page number
the etymology
questions.why: Etymology explains a word's origin.

questions.stem: In science class, to predict means to—
options: say what you think will happen
remember what happened in the past
count the numbers on the page
draw a picture of the result
questions.why: Predict means make a guess about what will happen.

questions.stem: Which word means to put things into groups?
options: classify
repeat
explain
describe
questions.why: Classify means sort into groups.

questions.stem: To compare two things means to—
options: tell how they are alike and different
count them and write down the number
pick a favorite and say why you like it
draw them on a big sheet of paper
questions.why: Compare looks at likenesses and differences.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The scientist will ____ the results to find patterns."
options: ignore
forget
decorate
analyze
questions.why: Analyze means study closely.

questions.stem: In "The data indicate that the plant grew faster in sunlight," what does indicate mean?
options: argue against
show or suggest
hide
measure
questions.why: Indicate means show.

questions.stem: Which word means a reason or proof that supports a claim?
options: title
opinion
evidence
guess
questions.why: Evidence supports claims.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The author's argument is ____ because she ignores important evidence."
options: valid
flawed
thorough
balanced
questions.why: Ignoring evidence makes an argument flawed.

questions.stem: In "The study's findings were inconclusive," what does inconclusive mean?
options: not leading to a firm result
very clear and easy to understand
surprising to the readers of it
false and full of mistakes
questions.why: Inconclusive means no firm conclusion.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a claim that can be checked with evidence?
options: vague
emotional
verifiable
fictional
questions.why: Verifiable means it can be checked.

questions.stem: Which word has a more positive feeling? The house was ____.
options: crowded
cramped
cozy
tiny
questions.why: Cozy sounds warm and nice.

questions.stem: Which word has a negative feeling?
options: stubborn
strong
determined
steady
questions.why: Stubborn suggests being difficult.

questions.stem: Slim and skinny both mean thin. Which sounds more positive?
options: skinny
slim
neither
both the same
questions.why: Slim has a more positive connotation.

questions.stem: Which word gives the most positive description of someone who saves money?
options: cheap
greedy
thrifty
stingy
questions.why: Thrifty suggests wise saving.

questions.stem: Which word suggests the speaker disapproves? "The child was ____ about the rules."
options: eager
curious
nosy
interested
questions.why: Nosy has a negative connotation.

questions.stem: Home and house have the same denotation. Why might a writer choose home?
options: It is shorter and easier to type.
It suggests warmth and belonging.
It is more formal and sounds official.
It means a bigger building with more rooms.
questions.why: Home carries emotional connotations.

questions.stem: A news report calls protesters "a mob" while another calls them "a crowd." How does the word choice differ?
options: Both words are neutral in tone and meaning to readers.
Crowd is a negative word for a group of people.
Mob is a positive word for a group of people.
Mob suggests disorder and danger; crowd is neutral.
questions.why: Mob has a negative connotation.

questions.stem: Which word choice would a writer use to make a politician seem admirable?
options: rigid
principled
inflexible
obstinate

to show a real game score from last week's big match
questions.why: Linking the cereal to winning athletes makes it seem powerful.

questions.passage: A TV commercial shows a smiling soccer team eating Crunch-O cereal. Loud, happy music plays. A voice says, "Champions start with Crunch-O!" The words "New Look! Same Great Taste!" flash on the screen.
questions.stem: What is the purpose of the loud, happy music?
options: to make viewers feel excited about the product
to warn people about too much sugar in the drink
to tell the price of the product today
to list the ingredients of the product
questions.why: Music sets a mood that makes the product seem fun.

questions.passage: A short video opens in slow motion: a bike tire wobbles on a wet road. The screen goes dark, and a single sound of a helmet tapping the ground is heard. Then a girl stands up, unhurt, and removes her helmet. Text appears: "It only takes one ride. Wear it every time." The video ends with the city's logo.
questions.stem: What is the main focus of the video's message?
options: Wet roads are fun to ride on in the rain.
Wearing a helmet on every ride protects you.
Bikes should be repaired often at the shop in town.
The city has a new logo for its sports teams.
questions.why: The closing text states the focus: wear a helmet every time.

questions.passage: A short video opens in slow motion: a bike tire wobbles on a wet road. The screen goes dark, and a single sound of a helmet tapping the ground is heard. Then a girl stands up, unhurt, and removes her helmet. Text appears: "It only takes one ride. Wear it every time." The video ends with the city's logo.
questions.stem: Why does the video use slow motion and a dark screen?
options: to show the bike's brand and its price to the viewers
to make the video longer than the other videos in class
to save money on filming and on the actors
to build tension so viewers feel the danger
questions.why: These techniques create suspense and emotion.

questions.passage: A short video opens in slow motion: a bike tire wobbles on a wet road. The screen goes dark, and a single sound of a helmet tapping the ground is heard. Then a girl stands up, unhurt, and removes her helmet. Text appears: "It only takes one ride. Wear it every time." The video ends with the city's logo.
questions.stem: How does showing the girl standing up unhurt support the message?
options: It proves bikes are never dangerous for any child who rides.
It shows the helmet's benefit without showing an injury.
It advertises a clothing store near the school.
It shows she won a race on her bike last week.
questions.why: The safe outcome shows what the helmet does.

questions.passageTitle: Two Ads for the Same Phone
questions.passage: Ad 1 (print): A detailed chart lists the phone's battery life (two days), camera resolution and price, beside a quote from a technology reviewer. Ad 2 (video): Teenagers laugh at a beach party, snapping photos, while upbeat music plays; the phone appears for three seconds at the end with the slogan "Don't miss a moment."
questions.stem: How do the two ads mainly differ in technique?
options: Both use the same expert quote about a famous brand of shoes and sports.
Both rely only on statistics and long tables of numbers and dates from the past.
Ad 1 appeals to logic with facts; Ad 2 appeals to emotion and belonging.
Ad 1 uses music and songs; Ad 2 uses a chart and many facts about the maker.
questions.why: Facts and expert opinion (logos) versus fun and friendship (pathos).

questions.passageTitle: Two Ads for the Same Phone
questions.passage: Ad 1 (print): A detailed chart lists the phone's battery life (two days), camera resolution and price, beside a quote from a technology reviewer. Ad 2 (video): Teenagers laugh at a beach party, snapping photos, while upbeat music plays; the phone appears for three seconds at the end with the slogan "Don't miss a moment."
questions.stem: Which audience is Ad 2 most likely designed for?
options: business owners buying many phones for their offices
engineers comparing technical details of the phone
young people who want to fit in and have fun
people who dislike music and loud sounds
questions.why: The party scene and slogan target teens' desire to belong.

questions.passageTitle: Two Ads for the Same Phone
questions.passage: Ad 1 (print): A detailed chart lists the phone's battery life (two days), camera resolution and price, beside a quote from a technology reviewer. questions.stem: What important information does Ad 2 leave out that a careful viewer should look for?
options: facts about the phone's features and price
how many people were at the beach that day
the color of the sky behind the people
the names of the songs in the ad
questions.why: Emotional ads often skip the facts a buyer needs.

sets.skill: Matching a Picture to a Definition

questions.stem: Which picture shows a fruit that is red or green, crunchy, and grows on a tree?
questions.why: An apple is a crunchy fruit that grows on a tree.

questions.stem: Which picture shows an animal that lives in water and has fins?
questions.why: A fish lives in water and swims with fins.

questions.stem: Which picture shows something you wear on your feet?
questions.why: Shoes are worn on your feet.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a thing you use to keep dry when it rains?
questions.why: An umbrella keeps you dry in the rain.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a tool that tells you what time it is?
questions.why: A clock shows the time.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a large vehicle that carries many people to school?
questions.why: A bus carries many students.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a tool used to see things that are very far away, like stars?
questions.why: A telescope helps you see faraway objects; a microscope shows tiny things.

questions.stem: Which picture shows something that helps you find which direction is north?
questions.why: A compass points north.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a building where sick people go to get care from doctors and nurses?
questions.why: A hospital is where doctors and nurses care for sick people.

questions.stem: Which word names a person?
options: quickly
teacher
happy
run
questions.why: A noun can name a person, such as teacher.

questions.stem: Which word names a place?
options: softly
jump
school
blue
questions.why: School is a place.

questions.stem: Which word names a thing?
options: slowly
tall
chair
sing
questions.why: A chair is a thing.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the noun correctly? "I put my ____ in my backpack."
options: books
fast
under
sleepy
questions.why: Books is a noun that fits the sentence.

questions.stem: Which word is a noun in this sentence? "The baby laughed."
options: none
laughed
the
baby
questions.why: Baby names a person.

questions.stem: Which word is the plural noun?
options: dogs
dug
dog
dig
questions.why: Adding -s makes dog plural: dogs.

questions.stem: Which group has only nouns?
options: quiet, river, friend
city, river, friend
run, jump, play
city, swim, friendly
questions.why: City, river and friend all name places, things or people.

questions.stem: Which word is a noun that names a feeling?
options: happen
happily
happy
happiness
questions.why: Happiness names a feeling, so it is a noun.

questions.stem: Choose the noun that best completes the sentence. "We bought milk and bread at the ____."
options: stormy
store
storing
stored
questions.why: Store is a noun naming a place.

questions.stem: How many syllables are in the word basket?
options: one
three
two (bas-ket)
four
questions.why: Bas-ket has two syllables.

questions.stem: How many syllables are in the word elephant?
options: two
four
one
three (el-e-phant)
questions.why: El-e-phant has three syllables.

questions.stem: Which word has only one syllable?
options: jump
jumpiness
jumper
jumping
questions.why: Jump has one vowel sound.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to divide the word napkin into syllables?
options: n-apkin
napk-in
nap-kin
na-pkin
questions.why: Divide between two consonants: nap-kin.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to divide the word tiger into syllables?
options: ti-ger
t-iger
tig-er
tige-r
questions.why: The first syllable ends with a long vowel: ti-ger.

questions.stem: Read the word unbelievable. Which shows its parts?
options: unb-el-ievable
un-be-liev-a-ble
u-nbeliev-able
unbe-lie-vable
questions.why: Prefix un-, root believe, suffix -able: un-be-liev-a-ble.

questions.stem: A student does not know the word misunderstanding. Which strategy helps most to read it?
options: look only at the first letter of the word
read it backward from the last letter
break it into parts: mis-under-stand-ing
skip it every time you see it in a text
questions.why: Prefixes, roots and suffixes make long words easier to decode.

questions.stem: Which word has a stressed first syllable?
options: PIC-ture
to-DAY
be-GIN
a-ROUND
questions.why: In picture, the first syllable is stressed.

questions.stem: How many syllables are in the word dictionary?
options: four (dic-tion-ar-y)
two
five
three
questions.why: Dic-tion-ar-y has four syllables.

questions.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as rain?
options: rug
ran
rip
play
questions.why: Ai in rain and ay in play make the long a sound.

questions.stem: Which letters make the sound /sh/ in the word ship?
options: sh
ip
hi
si
questions.why: The digraph sh makes one sound.

questions.stem: Which word has a silent letter?
options: nap
nest
net
knee
questions.why: The k in knee is silent.

questions.stem: In which word does ch sound like /k/?
options: cheese
lunch
school
chair
questions.why: In school, ch makes the /k/ sound.

questions.stem: Which word has the same ending sound as nation?
options: station
native
nature
notice
questions.why: -tion sounds like /shun/ in both nation and station.

questions.stem: Which word has a soft g, like in giant?
options: goat
game
gum
gem
questions.why: G before e often makes the soft /j/ sound.

questions.stem: Which word has the same sound for ough as in though?
options: cough
tough
dough
through
questions.why: Though and dough both have the long o sound.

questions.stem: The letters ph in photograph make which sound?
questions.why: Ph makes the /f/ sound.

questions.stem: Which word follows the rule: drop the final e before adding -ing?
options: be → being
make → making
play → playing
see → seeing
questions.why: Make drops the silent e before -ing.

questions.passageTitle: A Speech to the Student Council
questions.passage: "I think our school needs more water fountains. First, many students are thirsty after recess. Second, the lines at the two fountains are very long. Last week I counted 15 students waiting in one line!"
questions.stem: What is the speaker's main point?
options: Students should bring lunch from home to school.
The school needs more water fountains.
Recess should be longer than it is now.
The lines are fun and they move fast.
questions.why: The speaker's opening states the point.

questions.passageTitle: A Speech to the Student Council

questions.stem: Which reason does the speaker give?
options: The fountains are new and very clean.
The lines at the fountains are very long.
Water is boring to drink every day.
Fountains are expensive to build in a park.
questions.why: Long lines are one reason the speaker gives.

questions.passageTitle: A Speech to the Student Council

options: the speaker counted 15 students in one line
recess is fun for children at school
the speech was short and clear to follow
the speaker likes water and drinks it daily
questions.why: Counting students is evidence for the claim.

questions.passageTitle: Radio Talk: Should Our Town Build a Skate Park?
questions.passage: "A skate park would keep teens active and safe," said the speaker. "In nearby Riverton, a skate park opened two years ago, and police reports of skateboarding on sidewalks fell by half. Also, skating is great exercise. Some people say it will be too noisy, but the park would be next to the sports fields, far from homes."
questions.stem: Which claim is supported by specific evidence?
options: Skating is great exercise for kids and teens.
The park would be beautiful in the spring.
Everyone loves skating in the town park.
A skate park would keep teens safe.
questions.why: The Riverton police reports support the safety claim.

questions.passageTitle: Radio Talk: Should Our Town Build a Skate Park?

"In nearby Riverton, a skate park opened two years ago, and police reports of skateboarding on sidewalks fell by half. Also, skating is great exercise. Some people say it will be too noisy, but the park would be next to the sports fields, far from homes."
questions.stem: Which claim is NOT supported with evidence in the talk?
options: Sidewalk skating fell in Riverton.
Skating is great exercise.
The Riverton park opened two years ago.
The park would be far from homes.
questions.why: The speaker states it without giving evidence.

questions.passageTitle: Radio Talk: Should Our Town Build a Skate Park?

Some people say it will be too noisy, but the park would be next to the sports fields, far from homes."
questions.stem: How does the speaker respond to the noise concern?
options: by explaining the park would be far from homes
by agreeing to stop the project at once
by changing the topic to sports and school games
by ignoring it and not answering at all
questions.why: The speaker answers an opposing point with a reason.

questions.passage: "Homework should be limited to 30 minutes a night. A study of 2,000 students found that more than an hour of homework did not raise test scores. Furthermore, family time matters. My neighbor's kids are always stressed, so obviously all students are. Finally, the national teachers' association recommends shorter assignments for younger students."
questions.stem: Which piece of evidence is the weakest?
options: the neighbor's children are always stressed
the study of 2,000 students
the teachers' association recommendation
the claim about test scores
questions.why: One family cannot prove something about all students.

My neighbor's kids are always stressed, so obviously all students are. Finally, the national teachers' association recommends shorter assignments for younger students."
questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the speech?
options: Every claim has strong evidence, and the speaker proves each point clearly.
Most claims are supported by research, but one generalization is unsupported.
The speech has no claims, so there is nothing to judge or to check.
No claims are supported, and the speaker gives only opinions.
questions.why: The study and association are reliable; the neighbor example is a hasty generalization.

questions.passage: "Homework should be limited to 30 minutes a night. A study of 2,000 students found that more than an hour of homework did not raise test scores. Furthermore, family time matters. questions.stem: What could the speaker add to support the claim that family time matters?
options: research on how family time affects students' well-being
a longer list of homework subjects for every day of the week
a louder voice when he reads out the speech
the speaker's favorite TV show and his best cartoon
questions.why: Relevant research would support the unsupported claim.
